caseTitle: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) and Anr. v. Union of India and Ors.
bench: J.S. Khehar (CJI), J. Chelameswar, S.A. Bobde, R.K. Agrawal, R.F. Nariman, A.M. Sapre, D.Y. Chandrachud, S.K. Kaul, S. Abdul Nazeer
summary: A 9-judge Constitution Bench unanimously held that the right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and Part III freedoms.
judgmentText: The right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution. Privacy includes informational privacy and decisional autonomy. Any state intrusion into privacy must satisfy legality (existence of a valid law), a legitimate state aim, and proportionality.
officialSourceLabel: Supreme Court of India (Official Judgment PDF)
verificationNote: Verified directly against the official Supreme Court PDF (WP(C) No. 494 of 2012, dated 24 Aug 2017) and SCR publication.
article141Status: 9-Judge Constitution Bench — unanimous core ratio recognizing Article 21 privacy protection is binding under Article 141.
obiterAndScopeNote: Six concurring opinions articulate varied doctrinal tests; Chandrachud, Kaul, and Nariman JJ. formulate proportionality and data protection parameters.
subsequentTreatment: Applied in K.S. Puttaswamy (Aadhaar-5J) v. Union of India (2019) 1 SCC 1, Joseph Shine v. Union of India, and Navtej Singh Johar.
outcomeRationale: Overruled M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh to the extent they held privacy was not a fundamental right.

caseTitle: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
summary: The Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 as unconstitutionally vague and overbroad under Article 19(1)(a), while upholding Section 69A and reading down Section 79(3)(b).
judgmentText: Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 is struck down in its entirety for being violative of Article 19(1)(a) and not saved by Article 19(2). The Court distinguished between discussion, advocacy, and incitement, holding that only incitement to public disorder or offences falling under Article 19(2) can curtail speech. Under Section 79(3)(b), intermediary take-down obligations trigger only upon actual knowledge via court order or reasoned government notification.
verificationNote: Official SCI direct PDF URL could not be verified automatically; previous judis ID pointed to another judgment. Full judgment text verified on Indian Kanoon.
article141Status: Division Bench declaration under Article 32 striking down Section 66A IT Act is binding law nationwide under Article 141.
obiterAndScopeNote: Section 69A blocking mechanism was upheld because of procedural safeguards under the 2009 Blocking Rules.
subsequentTreatment: Supreme Court subsequently directed States and police in PUCL v. Union of India orders (2019–2021) to stop registering prosecutions under struck-down Section 66A.
outcomeRationale: Section 66A IT Act and Section 118(d) Kerala Police Act invalidated; Sections 69A and 79 upheld with safeguards.

caseTitle: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar and Anr.
bench: Chandramauli Kr. Prasad, Pinaki Chandra Ghose
summary: The Supreme Court prohibited automatic or mechanical arrests in offences punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years (including but not confined to Section 498A IPC), mandating adherence to Section 41 criteria and service of a Section 41A CrPC notice of appearance.
judgmentText: No arrest should be made routinely in offences punishable with imprisonment for a term up to seven years without satisfaction under Section 41(1)(b)(ii) CrPC recorded in writing and scrutinized by the Magistrate authorizing detention. Notice of appearance in terms of Section 41A CrPC must be served upon the accused within two weeks of institution unless extended for recorded reasons.
officialSourceLabel: Supreme Court of India (Official Judgment PDF)
verificationNote: Verified directly against official Supreme Court PDF (Criminal Appeal No. 1277 of 2014) and Andhra Pradesh HC SCR mirror.
article141Status: Mandatory arrest checklists and directions issued under Article 141 apply to all offences punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years.
obiterAndScopeNote: Factual origin involved Section 498A IPC, but Direction (11.7) expressly extends the guidelines to all offences punishable up to 7 years. For post-1 July 2024 cases, verify parallel requirements under Section 35 BNSS.
subsequentTreatment: Reaffirmed and extended in Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI (2022) 10 SCC 51 and Md. Asfak Alam v. State of Jharkhand (2023) 8 SCC 632.
outcomeRationale: Provisional bail granted and nationwide directions issued to curb mechanical arrests.

caseTitle: Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of U.P. and Ors.
bench: P. Sathasivam (CJI), B.S. Chauhan, Ranjana P. Desai, Ranjan Gogoi, S.A. Bobde
summary: A 5-judge Constitution Bench held that registration of an FIR is mandatory under Section 154 CrPC if the information discloses commission of a cognizable offence, permitting limited time-bound preliminary inquiry only in specified categories.
judgmentText: The registration of FIR is mandatory under Section 154 of the Code if the information discloses commission of a cognizable offence and no preliminary inquiry is permissible in such a situation. Where the information does not disclose a cognizable offence on its face, a limited time-bound preliminary inquiry (ordinarily within 7 days, later extended to 15 days / 6 weeks in exceptional cases) is permissible only in categories such as matrimonial, commercial, medical negligence, corruption, or abnormally delayed complaints.
verificationNote: Verified directly against official Supreme Court Reports SCR PDF hosted on Supreme Court S3WaaS server.
article141Status: 5-Judge Constitution Bench declaration binding under Article 141 for FIR registration norms; check Section 173 BNSS for post-1 July 2024 preliminary inquiry statutory provisions.
obiterAndScopeNote: Clarifies that mandatory FIR registration does not mandate automatic arrest of the accused.
subsequentTreatment: Preliminary inquiry timeline modified on 5 March 2014; statutory scheme updated under Section 173(3) BNSS (14-day inquiry for offences punishable between 3 and 7 years).
outcomeRationale: Constitution Bench settled mandatory registration rule under S. 154 CrPC.

caseTitle: Navtej Singh Johar and Ors. v. Union of India thr. Secretary Ministry of Law and Justice
bench: Dipak Misra (CJI), R.F. Nariman, A.M. Khanwilkar, D.Y. Chandrachud, Indu Malhotra
summary: A 5-judge Constitution Bench unanimously read down Section 377 IPC to decriminalize consensual sexual acts between adults in private, upholding constitutional morality over social majoritarianism.
judgmentText: Section 377 IPC, insofar as it criminalizes consensual sexual conduct between adults in private, is violative of Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(a) and 21 of the Constitution. Constitutional morality requires that dignity, equality, and sexual autonomy of individuals are protected. Section 377 continues to govern non-consensual sexual acts and acts against minors or bestiality (subject to legislative repeal/substitution under BNS 2023).
officialSourceLabel: Supreme Court of India (Official Judgment PDF)
verificationNote: Verified directly against official Supreme Court PDF (WP(Crl.) No. 76 of 2016, 495 pages).
article141Status: 5-Judge Constitution Bench ruling; binding under Article 141 on constitutional equality, manifest arbitrariness, and autonomy principles.
obiterAndScopeNote: Note that BNS 2023 omitted the general Section 377 IPC provision when commencing on 1 July 2024.
subsequentTreatment: Considered in Supriyo @ Supriya Chakraborty v. Union of India (2023).
outcomeRationale: Section 377 IPC read down to exclude consensual adult relationships.

caseTitle: Shayara Bano v. Union of India and Ors.
bench: J.S. Khehar (CJI), Kurian Joseph, R.F. Nariman, U.U. Lalit, S. Abdul Nazeer
summary: By a 3:2 majority, a 5-judge Constitution Bench set aside the practice of instantaneous irrevocable Triple Talaq (Talaq-e-Biddat) as invalid in law and manifestly arbitrary under Article 14.
judgmentText: Instantaneous and irrevocable talaq (talaq-e-biddat) allows the marital tie to be dissolved capriciously without attempt at reconciliation. Justices Nariman and Lalit held Section 2 of the 1937 Act enforcing talaq-e-biddat unconstitutional for manifest arbitrariness under Article 14, while Justice Kurian Joseph held the practice invalid under Muslim personal law lacking legislative sanctity.
verificationNote: Verified directly against official Supreme Court Reports SCR PDF on Supreme Court S3WaaS portal (362 pages).
article141Status: 3:2 Constitution Bench decision — binding ratio invalidates talaq-e-biddat and establishes manifest arbitrariness test for legislation (Nariman & Lalit JJ.).
obiterAndScopeNote: Minority opinion (Khehar CJI & Nazeer J.) differed on whether personal law is immune from Part III review.
subsequentTreatment: Followed by enactment of Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019.
outcomeRationale: Instantaneous triple talaq declared void.

caseTitle: Bir Singh v. Mukesh Kumar
summary: The Supreme Court held that if a signed blank cheque leaf is voluntarily handed over toward payment, the presumption under Section 139 NI Act applies even if particulars were subsequently filled in by the payee, unless rebutted by cogent evidence.
judgmentText: A meaningful reading of Sections 20, 87, and 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act establishes that a person who signs a cheque and hands it over to the payee remains liable under Section 138 unless evidence is adduced to rebut the presumption that it was issued in discharge of a debt or liability. Fiduciary relationship alone does not displace this statutory presumption.
verificationNote: Official SCI PDF link returned HTML rather than PDF. Full judgment text verified on Indian Kanoon.
article141Status: Division Bench ruling binding on Section 139 NI Act burden of proof regarding signed blank cheques.
obiterAndScopeNote: Rebuttal still remains open where the accused establishes absence of consideration or misuse beyond authority on a preponderance of probabilities.
subsequentTreatment: Followed alongside Rangappa v. Sri Mohan and Kalamani Tex v. P. Balasubramanian (2021) 5 SCC 283.
outcomeRationale: High Court acquittal reversed and conviction restored with enhanced compensation.

caseTitle: Rangappa v. Sri Mohan
bench: K.G. Balakrishnan (CJI), P. Sathasivam, J.M. Panchal
summary: A 3-judge bench settled that the statutory presumption under Section 139 NI Act extends to the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, and is rebuttable by the accused on a standard of preponderance of probabilities.
judgmentText: The presumption mandated by Section 139 of the Act does include the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability. Since the presumption is rebuttable, it is open to the accused to raise a probable defence wherein the existence of a legally enforceable debt can be contested on a preponderance of probabilities by relying on materials submitted by the complainant or defence evidence.
verificationNote: Official SCI direct PDF URL could not be verified. Full judgment text verified on Indian Kanoon.
article141Status: 3-Judge Bench authoritative ruling clarifying Krishna Janardhan Bhat (2008); binding law on Section 139 presumption.
obiterAndScopeNote: Accused does not necessarily have to enter the witness box to rebut the presumption if existing record creates probable doubt.
subsequentTreatment: Consistently followed in Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa (2019) 5 SCC 418 and Tedhi Singh v. Narayan Dass Mahant (2022) 6 SCC 735.
outcomeRationale: Conviction restored because accused did not establish a probable defence.

caseTitle: State of Haryana and Ors. v. Ch. Bhajan Lal and Ors.
bench: S. Ratnavel Pandian, K. Jayachandra Reddy
summary: Locus classicus laying down seven illustrative categories in which the High Court may exercise inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC (now Section 528 BNSS) or extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 226 to quash an FIR or complaint.
judgmentText: In exercise of extraordinary power under Article 226 or inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC, courts may quash criminal proceedings where allegations taken at face value do not prima facie constitute an offence, are absurd or inherently improbable, face an express legal bar, or are manifestly attended with mala fides instituted with ulterior motive to wreak vengeance.
verificationNote: Official SCI direct PDF URL could not be verified; earlier judis ID mapped to an unrelated ruling. Decision date corrected to 21 Nov 1990. Verified on Indian Kanoon.
article141Status: Leading Division Bench precedent guiding quashing jurisdiction nationwide; post-1 July 2024 petitions rely on Section 528 BNSS preserving inherent powers.
obiterAndScopeNote: The Supreme Court cautioned that quashing must be exercised sparingly without conducting a mini-trial at the threshold.
subsequentTreatment: Consistently applied in Neeharika Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra (2021) 19 SCC 401 and Iqbal @ Bala v. State of U.P. (2023).
outcomeRationale: Clarified limits on investigation interference while enumerating seven quashing categories.

caseTitle: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
bench: M.H. Beg (CJI), Y.V. Chandrachud, P.N. Bhagwati, V.R. Krishna Iyer, N.L. Untwalia, S. Murtaza Fazal Ali, P.S. Kailasam
summary: A 7-judge Constitution Bench established that any procedure depriving personal liberty under Article 21 must be fair, just, and reasonable—not arbitrary, fanciful, or oppressive—interlinking Articles 14, 19, and 21.
judgmentText: Procedure established by law under Article 21 cannot be any arbitrary procedure but must answer the test of fairness, justness, and reasonableness under Article 14 and natural justice. Articles 14, 19, and 21 form an integrated constitutional test rather than watertight compartments.
verificationNote: Official SCI direct PDF link not verified. Full 7-Judge Constitution Bench text verified on Indian Kanoon.
article141Status: 7-Judge Constitution Bench — foundational binding precedent on substantive due process, natural justice, and Article 21 liberty.
obiterAndScopeNote: Important specifically for arbitrary executive restrictions and denial of reasons/hearing, though post-decisional hearing may apply in urgent statutory exceptions.
subsequentTreatment: Foundational authority cited in Puttaswamy, Navtej Singh Johar, and arrest liberty rulings.
outcomeRationale: Impounding without reasons held contrary to natural justice and procedural fairness.

caseTitle: Vishaka and Ors. v. State of Rajasthan and Ors.
bench: J.S. Verma (CJI), Sujata V. Manohar, B.N. Kirpal
summary: In the absence of domestic statutory law at the time, a 3-judge bench framed mandatory guidelines under Articles 32 and 141 to prevent and redress sexual harassment of women at workplaces.
judgmentText: Sexual harassment at the workplace violates fundamental rights to gender equality and life with dignity under Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(g), and 21. Drawing upon Article 51(c) and CEDAW norms, the Supreme Court formulated binding workplace preventive and complaint mechanisms.
verificationNote: Official SCI direct PDF URL could not be verified automatically. Full text verified on Indian Kanoon.
article141Status: 3-Judge Bench directions functioned as law under Article 141 until legislative enactment of POSH Act, 2013.
obiterAndScopeNote: Now governed primarily by the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013.
subsequentTreatment: Codified into the POSH Act, 2013; interpreted in Aureliano Fernandes v. State of Goa (2023).
outcomeRationale: Mandatory guidelines promulgated pending parliamentary legislation.

caseTitle: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
summary: Laid down 11 mandatory procedural requirements during arrest and detention—including visible officer identification, contemporaneous attested arrest memo, medical inspection, and immediate intimation to a nominated relative or friend.
judgmentText: Custodial violence strikes at the rule of law. In every arrest or detention, police officers must prepare a memo of arrest attested by a witness and countersigned by the arrestee, inform a relative or friend nominated by the arrestee as soon as practicable, enter the details in the station diary, allow legal counsel access during interrogation (not throughout), and subject the arrestee to medical examination.
officialSourceLabel: Supreme Court of India (Official Judgment PDF)
verificationNote: Verified directly against official Supreme Court PDF (WP (Crl) No. 592 of 1987, dated 18 Dec 1996, 23 pages).
article141Status: Division Bench guidelines binding across India under Articles 21, 22, and 141; later codified into CrPC (2008 Amendment) and BNSS 2023.
obiterAndScopeNote: Arrest memo attestation, officer name tags, and relative/friend intimation apply uniformly irrespective of offence category. Statutory counterparts under BNSS 2023 include Sections 36 and 48.
subsequentTreatment: Codified via CrPC Amendment Act 2008 (Ss. 41B, 41C, 41D, 50A) and carried into BNSS 2023; reinforced in Paramvir Singh Saini v. Baljit Singh (2021) 1 SCC 184 (CCTV in police stations).
outcomeRationale: 11 mandatory custodial safeguards promulgated; custodial abuse condemned under Article 21.

caseTitle: Vidya Drolia and Ors. v. Durga Trading Corporation
bench: N.V. Ramana, Sanjiv Khanna, Krishna Murari
summary: A 3-judge bench laid down a four-fold test of non-arbitrability and held that landlord-tenant disputes governed by the Transfer of Property Act are arbitrable unless exclusively vested in special rent control forums.
judgmentText: A dispute is non-arbitrable when the cause of action and subject matter: (1) relates to actions in rem; (2) affects third-party rights with erga omnes effect; (3) relates to inalienable sovereign/public interest functions; or (4) is expressly or by necessary implication non-arbitrable under mandatory statutes. Referral courts at Section 8/11 stage exercise limited 'second look' prima facie review.
verificationNote: Official SCI direct URL returned HTML. Full text verified on Indian Kanoon and NLSIU PDF archive.
article141Status: 3-Judge Bench authoritative judgment governing subject-matter arbitrability and referral-stage scrutiny.
obiterAndScopeNote: Aspects concerning unstamped arbitration agreements were later reconsidered by a 7-Judge Constitution Bench in In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements under the A&C Act, 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 (2023 INSC 1066).
subsequentTreatment: Modified regarding unstamped agreements by 7-Judge Bench (2023 INSC 1066); four-fold non-arbitrability test continues to govern.
outcomeRationale: Tenancy disputes under TPA held arbitrable; Himangni Enterprises overruled.

caseTitle: Babu Singh and Ors. v. State of U.P.
caseIdentifier: Criminal Misc. Petition No. 1368 of 1977 in Criminal Appeal No. 43 of 1978
summary: Expounded humane bail jurisprudence emphasizing that refusal of an earlier bail plea does not bar a subsequent application upon changed circumstances, and that deprivation of personal liberty before final adjudication must serve legitimate trial ends.
judgmentText: Personal liberty of an accused or convict is fundamental and deprivation must reflect reasonable and legitimate considerations—chiefly securing presence for trial and preventing tampering with witnesses. Rejection of an earlier bail petition does not erect res judicata against renewing bail when relevant circumstances change.
verificationNote: Official SCI direct PDF URL could not be verified automatically. Full text verified on Indian Kanoon.
article141Status: Division Bench precedent regularly cited on successive bail maintainability and liberty principles.
obiterAndScopeNote: Bail entitlement always turns on offence gravity, custody duration, stage of trial, and risk of absconding/tampering.
subsequentTreatment: Cited extensively in State of Rajasthan v. Balchand, Sanjay Chandra v. CBI, and Satender Kumar Antil.
outcomeRationale: Bail granted on conditions pending appeal.

caseTitle: In Re: Cognizance for Extension of Limitation (Order dated 8 March 2021)
caseIdentifier: Suo Motu Writ Petition (Civil) No. 3 of 2020
bench: S.A. Bobde (CJI), L. Nageswara Rao, S. Ravindra Bhat
summary: In exercise of Article 142 powers during COVID-19 disruptions, the Supreme Court directed exclusion of the period from 15.03.2020 until 14.03.2021 in computing statutory periods of limitation across courts and tribunals (later further extended through 28.02.2022).
judgmentText: In computing the period of limitation for any suit, appeal, application or proceeding, the period from 15.03.2020 till 14.03.2021 shall stand excluded. Consequently, the balance period of limitation remaining as on 15.03.2020, if any, shall become available with effect from 15.03.2021.
officialSourceLabel: Supreme Court of India (Official Order PDF)
verificationNote: Verified directly against official Supreme Court order PDF dated 8 March 2021 (aligning date and Bench to (2021) 5 SCC 452).
article141Status: Article 142 binding pandemic limitation exclusion order (subsequently modified and concluded by final order dated 10 Jan 2022 excluding up to 28 Feb 2022).
obiterAndScopeNote: Relevant solely to limitation periods intersecting 15.03.2020–28.02.2022.
subsequentTreatment: Extended on 27 April 2021 and 23 Sept 2021; finalized on 10 January 2022 (excluding 15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022).
outcomeRationale: Pandemic limitation exclusion directions issued under Article 142.

caseTitle: Tata Sons Private Limited v. Hakunamatata Tata Founders & Ors.
summary: A Division Bench of the Delhi High Court allowed Tata Sons' appeal, holding that Indian courts may exercise territorial jurisdiction where foreign online crypto platforms deliberately target Indian users, and restrained unauthorized use of 'TATA Coin'.
judgmentText: Where websites hosted outside India offer interactive transactions and target Indian customers by trading cryptocurrency tokens bearing a well-known Indian trademark ('TATA'), purposeful availment supports territorial jurisdiction in India. Considering the well-known reputation of the TATA mark under Section 29, temporary injunction was warranted against infringement and passing off.
verificationNote: Previous Delhi HC ASP link returned HTTP 404 / timeout. Date, bench (Div. Bench 19 Sep 2022), and citation (2022 SCC OnLine Del 2968) verified; full text verified on Indian Kanoon.
article141Status: High Court Division Bench ruling — binding within Delhi High Court jurisdiction and persuasive across other High Courts.
obiterAndScopeNote: Jurisdictional test hinges on evidence of targeting / interactive commercial accessibility in India (Banyan Tree test).
subsequentTreatment: Division Bench reversed the Single Judge refusal and directed interim restraint.
outcomeRationale: Appeal allowed and ad-interim injunction granted against unauthorized trademark use.

caseTitle: Serum Institute of India Pvt. Ltd. and Anr. v. Yohan Tengra and Ors.
caseIdentifier: Interim Application (L) No. 33254 of 2022 in Suit (L) No. 33253 of 2022
legalProvisions: Order 39 Rules 1 & 2, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
summary: The Bombay High Court granted interlocutory relief in a civil defamation suit, holding that while fair public critique is protected speech, unsubstantiated, per se defamatory accusations causing reputational harm may warrant interim restraint.
judgmentText: Freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) does not confer licence to make reckless, unsubstantiated, per se defamatory imputations branding lawful entities or officers as murderers. Finding prima facie falsity and irreparable commercial reputational injury, the Court partly made the interim application absolute.
verificationNote: Official Bombay HC portal PDF URL timed out. Date, bench (R.I. Chagla J., 5 June 2023), and neutral citation corrected; verified on Indian Kanoon.
article141Status: Single Judge order of the Bombay High Court — persuasive authority on interlocutory defamation injunctions; governed by Bonnard v. Perryman standard.
obiterAndScopeNote: Subsequent proceedings involved platform takedown/IT Rules compliance orders.
subsequentTreatment: Interlocutory injunction granted; compliance/intermediary directions continued in 2023–2024.
outcomeRationale: Interim injunction granted restraining circulation of per se defamatory statements.

caseTitle: The State of Gujarat v. Sandip Omprakash Gupta
legalProvisions: Section 2(1)(c), Gujarat Control of Terrorism and Organised Crime Act, 2015 (GUJCOCA)
summary: The Supreme Court clarified the statutory definition of 'continuing unlawful activity' under GUJCOCA, holding that prosecution requires unlawful organized crime activity committed after the Act came into force, not merely historical pre-Act chargesheets.
judgmentText: To attract the offence of 'organised crime' under GUJCOCA (enforced 01.12.2019), an accused must engage in continuing unlawful activity as part of an organized crime syndicate, supported by more than one chargesheet in the preceding ten years AND an act amounting to organized crime committed after promulgation of the 2015 Act.
verificationNote: Official SCI direct PDF link returned HTML rather than PDF. Case identifier (Crl. A. No. 2291/2022) and bench (Nazeer & Pardiwala JJ.) corrected and verified against Indian Kanoon.
article141Status: Division Bench ruling interpreting special organized crime statutes against retrospective criminalization under Article 20(1).
obiterAndScopeNote: Also distinguishes state organized crime provisions (MCOCA/GUJCOCA) from ordinary IPC offences.
subsequentTreatment: State's appeal dismissed; GUJCOCA quashing affirmed.
outcomeRationale: State appeal dismissed; absence of post-commencement syndicate act barred GUJCOCA prosecution.

caseTitle: Anant Thanur Karmuse v. State of Maharashtra and Ors.
summary: The Supreme Court held that a victim has a fundamental right to a fair and impartial investigation under Article 21, and filing of a chargesheet does not bar constitutional courts from directing further investigation under Section 173(8) CrPC where warranted.
judgmentText: The victim has a fundamental right to fair investigation and fair trial. Even after submission of a chargesheet or framing of charges, constitutional courts are not denuded of power to order further investigation (or transfer/monitoring where warranted) to uncover the truth, though transfer to the CBI is reserved for rare and exceptional circumstances.
verificationNote: Official SCI direct PDF link returned HTML rather than PDF. Case identifier corrected to Criminal Appeal No. 13 of 2023 and verified on Indian Kanoon.
article141Status: Division Bench binding precedent under Article 141 regarding fair investigation and Section 173(8) CrPC (see Section 193(9) BNSS for post-1 July 2024 cases).
obiterAndScopeNote: Notice that transfer to CBI was declined, while further investigation by State CID/SIT was ordered.
subsequentTreatment: Reinforces fair victim participation principles settled in Jagjeet Singh v. Ashish Mishra (2022).
outcomeRationale: Appeal allowed in part; further investigation directed despite filing of chargesheet.

caseTitle: Associate Builders v. Delhi Development Authority
summary: A landmark Supreme Court judgment delineating the strictly confined scope of judicial interference with arbitral awards under Section 34, defining 'fundamental policy of Indian law', 'perversity', and 'patent illegality'.
judgmentText: Under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, a court does not sit in appeal over an arbitral award and cannot re-appreciate evidence. Construction of contractual terms is primarily for the arbitrator unless the view is impossible or perverse. Interference on grounds of 'public policy' is confined to narrow heads of illegality going to the root of the matter.
officialSourceLabel: Supreme Court of India (Official Judgment PDF)
verificationNote: Verified directly against official Supreme Court PDF (Civil Appeal No. 10531 of 2014, 48 pages). Replaced earlier unverified RIL entry.
article141Status: Foundational binding authority on Section 34 arbitration review; note statutory amendments in 2015 narrowed 'public policy' further (see Ssangyong Engineering (2019) 15 SCC 131).
obiterAndScopeNote: For post-2015 Amendment Act cases, 'patent illegality' is confined to Section 34(2A) for domestic awards and excludes international commercial arbitrations.
subsequentTreatment: Applied and refined in Ssangyong Engineering & Construction Co. Ltd. v. NHAI (2019) 15 SCC 131.
outcomeRationale: Division Bench interference set aside; arbitral award restored.

caseTitle: Union of India v. State of Maharashtra and Ors. (Review of Dr. Subhash Kashinath Mahajan)
bench: Arun Mishra, M.R. Shah, B.R. Gavai
legalProvisions: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
summary: A 3-judge bench in review recalled directions issued earlier in Dr. Subhash Kashinath Mahajan ((2018) 6 SCC 454) that had mandated preliminary inquiry and prior sanction before arrest under the SC/ST Act.
judgmentText: The directions issued under Article 142 requiring prior sanction for arrest of public servants/private persons and preliminary inquiry prior to FIR registration under the SC/ST Act were impermissible encroachments upon legislative domain and undermined statutory protections. Those directions are recalled.
verificationNote: Official SCI direct PDF link returned HTML. Case title corrected to 'Union of India v. State of Maharashtra' (the actual 2019 review decision reported at (2020) 4 SCC 761); verified on Indian Kanoon.
article141Status: 3-Judge Bench review judgment binding under Article 141; governs SC/ST Act threshold FIR & bail bar.
obiterAndScopeNote: Anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC / Section 482 BNSS remains barred under S. 18/18A SC/ST Act unless the complaint fails to make out any prima facie offence (Prathvi Raj Chauhan (2020) 4 SCC 727).
subsequentTreatment: Section 18A Amendment upheld in Prathvi Raj Chauhan v. Union of India (2020) 4 SCC 727.
outcomeRationale: Review allowed and restrictive 2018 arrest/inquiry directions recalled.

caseTitle: Salamat Ansari and 3 Ors. v. State of U.P. and 3 Ors.
court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
caseIdentifier: Criminal Misc. Writ Petition No. 11367 of 2020
summary: A Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court held that two consenting adults have a fundamental right under Article 21 to live together with a partner of their choice regardless of religion, quashing an FIR filed against an inter-faith couple.
judgmentText: Right to live with a person of his or her choice irrespective of religion professed by them is intrinsic to right to life and personal liberty under Article 21. Interference in a personal relationship between two individuals of majority constitutes a serious encroachment upon right to freedom of choice.
verificationNote: Replaced earlier unverified Smt. Saroj record whose Writ number could not be matched. Replaced with verified Allahabad High Court ruling Salamat Ansari v. State of U.P. (11 Nov 2020).
article141Status: High Court Division Bench ruling — binding in Uttar Pradesh and persuasive elsewhere; applies Shafin Jahan (SC).
obiterAndScopeNote: Requires proof that both individuals have attained age of majority and exercise free consent.
subsequentTreatment: Cited alongside Shafin Jahan v. Asokan K.M. (2018) 16 SCC 368.
outcomeRationale: FIR quashed protecting consenting adult partners' Article 21 liberty.

caseTitle: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation and Anr.
caseIdentifier: Miscellaneous Application No. 1849 of 2021 in SLP (Crl.) No. 5191 of 2021
summary: Comprehensive Supreme Court directions enforcing 'bail is the rule and jail is the exception', strictly mandating compliance with Sections 41 and 41A CrPC by investigating agencies and courts prior to authorizing remand or denying bail.
judgmentText: The investigating agencies and their officers are duty-bound to comply with the mandate of Section 41 and 41A of the Code and the directions issued in Arnesh Kumar. Any dereliction on their part has to be brought to the notice of higher authorities by the court. Courts considering bail must check compliance with Sections 41 and 41A; non-compliance entitles the accused to grant of bail.
officialSourceLabel: Indian Judiciary District Courts Portal (Official S3WaaS PDF)
verificationNote: Verified directly against circulated 85-page Supreme Court judgment PDF hosted on Delhi District Courts (S3WaaS) server and Indian Kanoon full text.
article141Status: Division Bench binding guidelines under Article 141 across all criminal courts in India; subsequently clarified to cover BNSS 2023 equivalent notice safeguards (Section 35 BNSS).
obiterAndScopeNote: Non-compliance with notice / arrest necessity rules under Section 41/41A (or Section 35 BNSS) is a central ground for regular bail and challenging mechanical remand, without assuming automatic anticipatory bail.
subsequentTreatment: Supreme Court continues monitoring compliance across High Courts; explicitly linked to Section 35 BNSS in subsequent compliance orders (2024–2025).
outcomeRationale: Comprehensive bail and Section 41/41A arrest-compliance framework issued.

caseTitle: Pankaj Bansal v. Union of India and Ors.
legalProvisions: Section 19(1), Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002
summary: Held that informing an arrested person of the grounds of arrest under Article 22(1) and Section 19 PMLA requires furnishing the written grounds of arrest to the arrestee as a matter of course, rendering oral reading insufficient.
judgmentText: To give true meaning and purpose to the constitutional and statutory mandate of Section 19(1) of the PMLA read with Article 22(1) of the Constitution, a copy of the written grounds of arrest must be furnished to the arrested person as a matter of course and without exception. Remand Magistrates must verify compliance before authorizing custody.

caseTitle: Prabir Purkayastha v. State (NCT of Delhi)
caseIdentifier: Criminal Appeal No. 2577 of 2024 (SLP (Crl.) No. 4289 of 2024)
summary: Extending Pankaj Bansal under Article 22(1), the Supreme Court held that grounds of arrest (distinguished from mere 'reasons to arrest') must be communicated in writing at the earliest, and failure vitiates both initial arrest and subsequent remand orders even after filing of chargesheet.
judgmentText: There is a vital distinction between 'reasons for arrest' (general formal parameters in an arrest memo) and 'grounds of arrest' (specific personal factual allegations informing the arrestee why custody is necessary). Under Article 22(1), grounds of arrest must be communicated in writing to enable consultation with counsel and opposition to remand. Failure renders the arrest and subsequent remand void ab initio, uncured by filing a chargesheet.

caseTitle: Vihaan Kumar v. State of Haryana and Anr.
bench: Abhay S. Oka, Nongmeikapam Kotiswar Singh
summary: Held in an ordinary IPC criminal offence (cheating/fraud) that communicating grounds of arrest only to relatives or noting them in general police diaries does not satisfy Article 22(1); meaningful direct communication to the arrestee is mandatory, failing which arrest and subsequent remand orders become illegal.
judgmentText: The requirement under Article 22(1) to inform the arrested person of the grounds of arrest is mandatory across all criminal arrests, including ordinary IPC/BNS offences. Intimating a spouse or relative (under S. 50A CrPC / S. 48 BNSS) serves a distinct purpose and does not substitute for direct communication of the grounds to the arrestee in an intelligible language. Once violation of Article 22(1) is established, subsequent remand or chargesheet does not validate illegal detention.

caseTitle: Mihir Rajesh Shah v. State of Maharashtra and Another
summary: Clarified and standardized Article 22(1) and Section 47 BNSS compliance for all general penal offences, directing prospectively that written grounds of arrest must be furnished in a language understood by the arrestee at least two hours prior to production before the Magistrate for remand.
judgmentText: Reading Article 22(1) harmoniously with Section 50 CrPC and Section 47 BNSS, the Supreme Court held that grounds of arrest must be furnished in writing to the arrestee across all offences under the IPC/BNS (not merely special statutes) in a language understood by the arrestee, and ordinarily at least two hours prior to production before the Magistrate for remand, operating prospectively.
